A novel logistic equation variant, acting as a cell biology model, is analyzed to study its global dynamics based on the presence or absence of a specific parameter threshold. The model's solution exhibits non-convergence towards a single equilibrium due to unbounded growth, prompting the use of conventional mathematical modeling methods to study its temporal evolution. The approach employed utilizes a time delay to modulate the model's behavior, incorporating a key parameter that significantly impacts global dynamics. The solution strategy involves transforming the delay equation into an infinite system of ordinary differential equations, represented as an ordered state space. The global attractor formed by the system's orbits can be fully described based on the model's parameter settings, allowing for the identification of resulting patterns and structures.

The use of statistical depths has become increasingly popular for evaluating and differentiating the efficiency of animal sampling designs. Recent studies have focused on developing depths for compositions that represent portions of data with various interpretations, including percentages, proportions, and log-ratio values. This paper presents a new method for defining depths on the composition space without explicitly accounting for its geometric properties. Instead, it applies the isometric log-ratio transformation to convert compositions into lower-dimensional Euclidean space, where established methods for analyzing and interpreting data can be employed. The transformed data are then compared using standard depth measures such as depths based on orthonormal vectors or marginal depths. The proposed approach offers advantages over other depth measures by allowing for the incorporation of skip-zero transformations, enabling the comparison of samples with zero-observed variables, and facilitating the focus on non-zero-observed variables when present. Ultimately, the chosen sampling design is selected by evaluating the median depth and related properties of the test data after applying the isometric log-ratio transformation.

A particular class of materials known as high-temperature superconductors, specifically made from rare-earth and transition-metal elements, exhibit unique properties in both their electrical conductivity and magnetic properties. When these materials are very cold and conduct electrical current, any attempt to disrupt this current flow will result in an instant, complete failure of the current; this is true for both the current flow and magnetic field interactions. Furthermore, the very weak interplay between electrical conductivity and magnetism in these materials can be modeled with high precision, making them ideal for use in extremely sensitive magnetic sensors and measurement tools. In a new research study, this team explored the magnetic properties of a specific type of device that uses these materials and an alternative superconductor, exhibiting exceptional agreement with predicted results. The discovered magnetic responses in this device also offer potential applications for the detection and analysis of both extremely weak magnetic fields and rapid, high-frequency magnetic vibrations.

To study the isomerism and radiation-driven reaction mechanism in Germanium isotopes, a Gas-Wall-Center $\beta$-delayed proton emitter technique was employed. By measuring the half-lives and proton emission spectra of even-even and odd-odd Germanium isotopes, specific knowledge about their properties was gained. This information included the nuclear energy levels, decay modes, and the mass of the isotopes, which enabled researchers to evaluate the nuclear energy surface and the isospin-dependent mass tensor for this region of the nuclear chart. Comparing experimental results with different theoretical models revealed that the isospin-symmetric and semi-empirical mass models provide the most accurate predictions. Moreover, the study of odd-odd Germanium isotopes offered insight into the structure of their excited states at zero spin, while the analysis of even-even isotopes provided knowledge of their nuclear quadrupole deformation.

A new technique for accurately measuring the masses of very short-lived, unusual isotopes has been developed using the precision Penning trap mass spectrometry method. This method relies on the Penning trap's ability to trap ions for a long time, allowing for the measurement of their mass many times over a short period. By taking advantage of a radio-frequency oscillator, the magnetic field in the trap can be adjusted rapidly at a rate determined by the mass being studied and the electric charge. When an isotope of interest is overlaid with a well-known reference isotope under a static magnetic field, the isotope's mean beat period in the trap is directly proportional to their mass difference. This period can be accurately measured many times over a short period and is then used to calculate the mass of the studied isotope. We tested this method by making an accurate measurement of the mass of the isotope $^{46}$K using $^{40}$K as a reference isotope. The result of our study is in agreement with the existing data studied by the TPC/X-U-1200 Penning trap at the University of Mainz, and our new method has the potential to make precise measurements of many previously hard-to-reach isotopes.

In recent years, there's been a significant surge in the development of new algorithms to simulate lattice field theories. This has led to an increased diversity in methods being used to tackle complex many-body problems. A key challenge lies in ensuring that these different algorithms produce results consistent with the laws of quantum mechanics, especially when the number of digital observations exceeds one million. This is where Standardizing Flows come into play, providing a unified framework that bridges multiple approaches and facilitates accurate predictions. This document serves as a comprehensive guide to implementing SFlows within lattice field theory for the simulation of finite temperature QCD, using an approach inspired by Variational Gaussian Habitat.

This research introduces a novel approach to improve the recognition of structured text within images by leveraging the characteristics of regular expressions. A database of regular expression patterns and corresponding text representations has been created, allowing the model to distinguish favorable expressions during training. A subsequent demonstration of the efficacy of this approach is shown in the application of handwritten ticket recognition.

The production of top-anti-top quarks pairs in proton-nucleus collisions has been examined. A theoretical framework for predicting the production of these quarks in such collisions has been introduced. It includes terms that arise from primary interactions and also from initial nucleon-nucleon interactions that have not yet been resolved. By considering the rapid decay time of top quarks, the examination has specifically looked at the production of these quarks at the Large Hadron Collider using a 13 TeV proton lead beam. The predictions based on a simplified theoretical model have been presented. They include calculations of the production of these quarks based on both leading-order and next-to-leading-order perturbative QCD models. The examination has also compared these predictions with experimental data from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. The examination has particularly looked at the distribution of events with high transverse momentum imbalance. The examination has also ascertained the influence of non-linear small x saturation effects in parton distribution functions on the production of these quarks. The predictions based on a simplified theoretical model have specifically stated the expected production of these quarks in proton lead collisions. The examination has particularly looked at the production of these quarks in events with high transverse momentum for the lead nucleus. The examination has particularly looked at the production of these quarks in events with high transverse momentum for the top quark. The examination has particularly looked at the production of these quarks in events with high transverse photon momentum.

Our proposed system approaches the challenge of evaluating semantic meaning in natural language as a question-answering task. It analyzes text to identify queries that can be framed as SQL requests and considers various factors such as column references, logical operators, and logical entities like aggregation functions and sorting mechanisms. To enhance our system's ability to understand the nuances of natural language, we've incorporated the analysis of syntactic structures, lexical vocabulary, and logical entities associated with column names. During training, our system is optimized using a multi-task framework that evaluates its linguistic accuracy by comparing its predicted outputs with expert-written SQL code drawn from different domains. When testing, its performance is measured by its ability to accurately translate a wide range of spontaneous language into SQL code across different domains. Our system has been validated through analysis and benchmarking on existing datasets, demonstrating superior performance and a more detailed layer-by-layer breakdown of its processing capabilities.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand how the development of galaxies relates to large-scale structures and radio luminosity. By analyzing data from the first release (at 65-75 MHz) for a specific region of 5.2 square degrees in the Northern sky, this study starts to explore these connections within a relatively small, dense area of sky. To calculate the energy spectrum of galaxies, the data is initially corrected for bias and selection effects. Based on this corrected spectrum, this study investigates LoTSS source bias and the connection between radio luminosity and space density, finding evidence of significant bias at high radio luminosities in the LoTSS catalog (> 3x10^26 W Hz^-1). Using LoTSS data, this study also constructs galaxy bias parameters, such as $b_{\rm LoTSS}$ and $b_{\rm LoTSS,2}$, which help characterize this bias across various ranges of radio luminosity. Furthermore, this study compares LoTSS bias parameters with those from the XXL cluster catalog, revealing an interesting connection between radio luminosity and space density that could provide valuable insights into galaxy evolution.

A comprehensive model for analyzing data ranking has been developed using Bayesian linear regression models. This data model can be interpreted as a factor model with variables ranked in a specific order. Our study focuses on a related optimization problem, known as the ranking lasso problem, which is crucial for making informed data analysis decisions. To tackle this issue, we introduce an new algorithm based on an adaptive sieving approach, which is fast, efficient, and handles large datasets easily. Compared to the existing best methods, our approach significantly outperforms it in terms of computational speed and successfully handles large-scale data problems.

We examine the entropy production of a particle in an optical cavity, driven by irregularly timed, weak forces. To analyze this, we apply the convex entropy representation, enabling us to derive lower bounds for the entropy production at any given time. This approach allows us to break down the averaging process in two distinct ways, as initially taking the average over an infinite number of driving events leads to a convergent result, and subsequently averaging over a finite number of events yields a quantifiable error. Furthermore, for driven systems exhibiting underdamped dynamics, we develop a convex program for estimating the entropy production rate; this rate converges to the correct value as the number of events increases. We also explore the limitations of entropy decay rates in response to various types of driving mechanisms, including randomly timed and weakly forced conditions.

Several environmental issues are being tackled with the aid of artificial intelligence, reducing the adverse effects of AI on the environment in the long term. However, the positive impact of AI is often hindered by its high energy requirements, which are usually met by non-renewable power sources. This research assessed the ecological impact of eight AI-driven solutions for real-world problems, taking into account the energy used to support them. The analysis considered various factors such as energy sources, device efficiency, data storage, and data processing. The results reveal that some applications, like image recognition, are still dependent on outdated technologies despite having alternative low-carbon solutions available, while others, such as sound classification, can benefit from the continued development of more energy-efficient alternatives. The study identified compute paradigms, like edge computing, that can minimize energy-related losses. Ultimately, the research suggests that a combination of technological advancements and computational strategies can help alleviate the negative effects of AI, and the only path to significantly reducing AI's carbon footprint is to fully transition to renewable energy sources.

Prescriptive Process Monitoring, which provides early warnings of potential issues by identifying problematic procedures, is heavily reliant on procedure models to function effectively. However, extracting and accurately modeling real processes from actual business data proves to be a significant challenge due to the inherent noise and inconsistencies in the data. This sets a high standard for a procedure model to perform well, which is difficult to achieve when relying on data mining methods that are susceptible to degradation over time. This raises the concern of how relevant and useful the warnings and predictions provided by Prescriptive Process Monitoring systems really are. This paper investigates the extent to which PP-M, a framework for Prescriptive Process Monitoring, can detect and prevent problematic procedures with high accuracy, using actual enterprise data. The results show that PP-M struggles to provide accurate warnings and predictions for procedures with low frequencies, which raises doubts about the effectiveness of PP-M in providing proactive warnings. The implications of these findings suggest that Process Mining methods may be limited in their ability to support proactive Process Monitoring.

A novel approach utilizing the Weak Reference Model, which is based on the Boussinesq equation, is developed to solve problems involving heat transfer and mass transport. This method is designed to ensure that the difference between the Weak Reference Model and a highly accurate reference solution remains within a predetermined error limit. To achieve this, a dynamic adaptation algorithm is implemented that adjusts key parameters in the Weak Reference Model until the desired accuracy is achieved. This approach is successfully tested on complex geometries and flow scenarios and is shown to effectively regulate error levels.

In algorithmic satisfiability theory, kernelization is a parameter-reducing operation. It lessens the size of an instance of a problem, yet maintains its solvability, while retaining the solution to the original instance. This operation is applicable to instances of NP-complete problems, specifically those with fixed-parameter tractability. Until now, no one has explored kernelization in the context of stacking problems, which are defined as follows: Given a set of rectangular plates stacked on top of one another, determine if they can be balanced without tipping over. This is a well-studied NP-complete problem with fixed-parameter tractability. Our contribution is the development of kernelization for this problem, specifically for its planar and convex variants, both of which have the same level of complexity. This achievement is based on a combination of techniques, including reduction by contraction, reduction by deletion, and reduction by substitution. These operations reduce the size of an instance while preserving its solution. Our kernelization results show that the size of an instance can be decreased to $O(c^q)$, where q is the number of layers in the stack, and c is a constant that depends on the specific problem variant. These results are crucial for answering query questions regarding stacking instances efficiently.

This paper explores how social connections and personal beliefs evolve in a network of individuals with diverse opinions, where each person has the option to switch to a different group if the prevailing view there differs significantly from their own. We have developed a mathematical model that incorporates both the dynamics of opinion change and group membership changes. Our analysis reveals the existence of multiple equilibrium states in the system, including situations where a single group holds all members. We have determined the specific conditions necessary for the stable coexistence of multiple groups with members holding diverse opinions. We have also identified key factors that can lead to a situation where one group dominates and all other members switch to it. We have developed a mathematical concept to quantify the level of confidence in a group's view and found that this confidence is limited by a maximum amount. We have further derived formulas that estimate the lower and upper bounds of confidence, and these results have been verified through numerical simulations.

A type of star known as a black star is being studied, which is in a state of equilibrium and has mass and charge properties.  This particular black star is classified as both essentially level and essentially hairy, due to its unique characteristics.  We have performed a detailed analysis of the interior region of this asymptotically flat black hole.  Our findings show that the interior structure of this black star consists of multiple layers separated by the phase transitions of its charge.  Additionally, its metric properties are significantly affected by its charge state.  This specific example illustrates that a black star can exhibit both bare and hairy properties, and our study delves into the interior geometry of these entities.

Live cell imaging has shown that transcription in human cells occurs
simultaneously with RNA transport but little is known about the time delay
between transcription start and RNA appearance. In order to investigate this
issue, researchers used genome-wide data to create a model of RNA production 
and opted for a statistical approach that relied on spatial information, 
avoiding the need for assumptions about RNA transport. The results indicate 
that the time delay between transcription start and RNA appearance is around 
five minutes and that longer RNAs experience greater delays. The research 
divides genes into categories based on the time delay and finds that 
coordinating transcription with spindles is not sufficient to explain these 
patterns. The findings are consistent with experimental data from Purfield et 
al. (2017), suggesting a model of transcription regulation that is controlled 
primarily by the structure of target genes.

Researchers studying the nucleus 64Ni, specifically its isospin-T=0 rotation-vibration collective state, have gained new insights due to data analyzed from 70Zn + 64Ni experiments conducted at GSI's storage ring. These insights reveal detailed level structures for 64Ni's rotational-vibration states, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of its phase transition and ground states. A theoretical model incorporating tensor interactions is presented, providing a satisfactory explanation for the observed structural changes.

We examine various chiral gauge theories that might serve as contenders in non-supersymmetric dualities to M-theory or string theory. By leveraging the power of holography from the Peierls mechanism to 't Hooft, we can identify distinct chiral theories corresponding to the same bulk dual. We explore integral and half-integer level large $N$ SO(2N+1) gauge theories as well as USp(2N) theories with unique features in their spectral gaps and flavor representations that enable us to propose them as bulk duals to various wrapped M2-branes configurations in string theory. We also discuss the distinct chiral theories for the free fermion and Yang-Mills phases of SO(2N+1) gauge theories, where the spectral gap transitions into a flavor gap, and where we identify a class of theories that are dual to each other in trips of four with SO(2N+1) symmetry in the bulk.

A linear complementary set of group codes is defined as a collection of group codes whose intersection contains only the zero element. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of such sets under specific parameter constraints and provide explicit constructions in particular scenarios. Additionally, our findings are framed within the broader context of set coincidences between group codes.

Graphical models offer a unified framework for continuous and discrete problems, enabling the exploration of intricate relationships within complex systems. However, applying these models to real-world issues often involves significant computational hurdles, particularly when dealing with large datasets or complex domains. Even simpler models can introduce numerical optimizations that are computationally intensive, making them hard to solve exactly. In this work, we introduce a new representation technique that allows for an efficient and precise description of the model's constraints, leading to a faster exact solution for Maximum Probability/Utility Problems and related optimization tasks. By providing a more concise and structured depiction of the model's domain, our approach offers improved performance for solving these problems, outperforming established within-tree clustering methods and offering superior results for large-scale datasets.

When a person drops an object, optical features may not immediately reflect the event's dynamics because the camera may not be directly aligned with the dropped item. However, acoustic cues can provide initial clues. To coordinate audio and visual information, a coordinated representation is created by combining the two modalities. If the time difference between the audio and visual cues is deemed acceptable, considered within a set tolerance, the two cues are re-synchronized and re-integrated. This process enables more precise tracking and ultimately allows for the detection of the dropped item.

When a viscoelastic fluid is subjected to rapid strain rates, its viscosity plummeting can transition into an even more extreme scenario known as shear thickening collapse, characterized by an abrupt and drastic increase in viscosity that outstrips typical shear thickening phenomena by orders of magnitude. Despite initial reports of universal power-law scaling for all types of shear thickening behaviors, research has revealed that different types of shear thickening can exhibit distinct scaling behaviors when subjected to varying strain amplitudes, leading to a call for reevaluating the universal nature of shear thickening transitions. This study provides a comprehensive examination of shear thickening collapse and other types of shear thickening transitions using a database of 174 experimental measurements across a range of polymer-based liquids. Our research reveals a systematic variation in scaling exponents across different types of shear thickening transitions and uncovers a hidden pattern in these transitions, showing that the scaling exponent for shear thickening collapse is consistently lowest and is consistently highest for shear thickening transitions involving liquid crystals. Moreover, by utilizing principal component analysis to identify patterns in the data, we have developed a theoretical framework that underpins a new understanding of the different types of shear thickening transitions and their relationships.

This study investigates electricity consumption patterns in Ghana's phase of power deficiency by examining hourly readings from the national grid monitoring system over a three-year period. The findings show that electricity usage is bimodally distributed, with analysis indicating two distinct patterns - one dominant peak at the end of each working day and a secondary, less prominent peak in the early hours of each day. The primary peak is attributed to evening usage, while the secondary peak is linked to overnight recharging of customers' meters. By comparing daily usage patterns during power crises and normal periods, this study reveals reduced overall consumption during power shortages, as well as altered hour-by-hour patterns with decreased usage in non-peak hours and increased usage in peak hours during power crises. The study employs Bayesian inference, incorporating seasonality and trend analysis to model hourly consumption and identify significant variations throughout the year and across different days of the week.

A crucial concept in knowledge management involves the relationship between a query, the relevant information, and the individual executing the search. Yet, little research has been conducted on how the searcher interacts with query-relevant information on the web. Our study innovates by investigating the effects of two prominent factors influencing searchers: generic search skills and personal connections with search engines. We demonstrate that searchers' perceptions of available information can vary significantly depending on their relationship with search engines, as demonstrated by substantial discrepancies between human and algorithmic judgments of encountered information. Our results indicate that searchers with established search histories may fail to recognize up to 29% of relevant information, while searchers without pre-existing connections with search engines may miss up to 41% of such information. These outcomes suggest that searchers could profit from training in search skills to minimize missed information in the digital realm.

Automating the process of creating programs from flow diagrams has long been a goal for programmers, and a key challenge lies in accurately interpreting the graphical elements and their connections within these diagrams. To address this issue, we propose GRCNN, a novel deep learning network designed to recognize and interpret the relationships within diagrams. By taking a flow diagram as input, GRCNN generates the corresponding Java code as output. Our research involved analyzing data from the 1990 MICE competition, and the results show that GRCNN significantly improves performance when combined with a recurrent neural network compared to the existing top-performing method.

Diminution techniques, such as data filtering and feature extraction, play a significant role in climate research by facilitating the exploration of complex high-dimensional datasets. This report provides an overview of filtering methods, including both linear and nonlinear techniques, and highlights their applications in climate science for both data analysis and model forecasting. The report also examines various evaluation metrics used to assess the performance of diminution techniques and provides case studies of their utilization in real-world climate applications.

Recent discoveries of kilonovae have led to a surge in studying the relativistic multiply ionized ions produced in these events, with a primary focus on the superdense object formed through neutron star mergers. Although initial advancements have been made, there remains a significant lack of data available for the most crucial ions in the most advanced stages of these phenomena. Specifically, an essential missing link has been the atomic information required for the Os-like ions necessary for accurately understanding the most extreme kilonova ejecta. Our paper presents the most comprehensive atomic data for the Os isoelectronic sequence in the Au IV stage, featuring energy levels, radiative rates, and probabilities of electron relaxation, as well as recombination rates and recurrence relationships. Our results are accurate to an unprecedented precision, with a relative error of less than one part in one million. Our data is further supplemented with the results of multiconfiguration relativistic atomic structure calculations, which provide a wealth of information on the atomic structure of the Os isoelectronic sequence. Our results are expected to be invaluable in understanding the behavior of ions in the most intense astrophysical environments, including kilonovae and hypernovae, as well as in the most extreme terrestrial particle beam facilities.

Deep learning technology has significantly improved the accuracy and efficiency of image processing. Although its application in gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is still emerging, this study leverages a state-of-the-art deep learning model to develop an automated small intestine extraction algorithm for endoscopy. By integrating the extracted small intestine mask into a unified belly-net model, we achieved comprehensive GI canal segmentation. Both ellipse-based and mask-based approaches were employed to derive cephalic, abdominal, and pelvic regions from the belly-net output. Our automated GI canal segmentation superimposed onto abdominal CT scans outperformed human-derived masks in terms of dice score, with results indicating high generalization for the segmentation of gastrointestinal structures.

We analyze information presented in linear form, focusing on the composition, to determine the time-dependent relationships between multiple variables. This requires a methodical approach to data interpretation, ensuring that the selected variables and their relationships are accurately represented. To achieve this, we utilize techniques such as dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and model identification to derive a simplified expression for variable relationships, which can then be visually inspected to gain insights. Our approach is illustrated using various industrial and environmental case studies.

The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS has been used to test a theoretical model proposing a 'desert' of low-mass inner planets resulting from core-mass growth and planetary volatility preservation during migration. Analyzing the dataset, researchers found no evidence to support this 'desert' around main-sequence stars. In fact, they found a higher than expected occurrence of sub-Saturn mass inner planets within a specific radius range. This discrepancy may be attributed to several factors such as planetary volatility being lost or core-melting thresholds being surpassed. Alternatively, it is possible that the 'desert' phenomenon is hidden within the dataset and can be revealed by focusing on planets around low-mass stars.

To enhance the robustness of Attention networks, which are highly sensitive to adversarial input, we develop a novel regularization technique called TRBM. This method derives inspiration from the principles of information theory, specifically the idea of maximizing shared information among input, features, and outputs. By doing so, TRBM strengthens the model's parameters and helps them resist manipulation. Unlike traditional techniques that rely on random input flaning or gradient-based attacks, TRBM can be applied both before and after training, making it a versatile tool for improving the model's resilience. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that TRBM achieves significant improvements in the model's robustness, with an average boost of 1.03% and 1.14% for CNN and RNN networks, respectively, without compromising accuracy or computational resources.

In models of dark matter that involve compressed matter, YDM, the interaction between dark matter particles is mediated by a Yukawa force. This force has a significant impact on the dark matter binding energy, especially in the near field, where it may overcome the repulsive force and result in a more stable nucleus. We are examining a wide range of YDM models with varying repulsive forces, as well as compressed dark matter models, including both canonical and extended scalar sectors. Our analysis reveals that a specific parameter space region, characterized by a low dark matter mass and a strong Yukawa interaction, leads to a long-range equilibrium of dark matter nuclei within a few hundred kilometers. We are estimating the YDM nucleus lifetime in order to identify potential signals and connections to other theories, such as the Baryon Asymmetry Maximum Entropy Theory. Our study also explores possible evidence for YDM nuclear states in X-ray searches and direct dark matter detection experiments.

Neural networks trained with sparse connections can solve various tasks more efficiently, despite the added complexity, by reducing unnecessary information transfer. By applying this concept to recurrent neural networks (RNNs), we observed that moderately sparse models often yield better results than traditional, fully connected networks. To mimic biological neurons' properties, we used a fixed and deterministic synaptic connection scheme, resulting in an unexpected improvement - sparse models typically took fewer training steps to reach the same performance level as fully connected networks. When applying these models to multiple cognitive tasks, we found they achieved superior outcomes with fewer training episodes. Our findings support the idea that simpler, more biological-inspired models can excel in complex cognitive tasks.

We establish a comprehensive classification of nilpotent algebras in a specific dimension based on their geometric properties. Our findings also address the question of whether every nilpotent algebra can be decomposed into non-split tori, providing a positive answer. Additionally, we derive exact counts of the number of tori in each category, matching these counts with existing results from the literature.

Active galactic nuclei with massive black holes at their center emit powerful energy across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, spanning from extremely large scales of hundreds of thousands of kilometers to tiny regions measuring mere micrometers. Strong gravitational force allows these black holes to pull nearby matter, accelerating it in the process and producing high-speed jets that travel billions of kilometers and shine with incredible energy. Research suggests that supermassive black holes at the center of galaxies existed more than 13 billion years ago, even before the cosmic dawn. It has been hypothesized that they likely resided within massive galaxies, similar to those seen in the Hubble Canyon of the cosmos. This research aims to investigate how large black holes influence the development of their host galaxies through observations of cosmic microwave background radiation at the edge of the observable universe. Using advanced computer simulations, it is simulated how cosmic microwave background radiation affects the growth of galaxies and their central black holes over 200 million years, particularly during the early stages of a hypothetical galaxy similar to those seen in the Hubble Canyon of the cosmos. This simulation considers various factors such as the black hole's jet energy, its intensity, and how it affects nearby hot plasma, all while accounting for common astronomical phenomena. The results show that cosmic microwave background radiation has a negligible impact on the host galaxy's overall development, but significantly affects the emission of relativistic jets, ultimately leading to an reduced intensity. This outcome contradicts earlier predictions made by other researchers. This new information could be integrated into existing theoretical

We examine various methods of forming Lagrangians for classical gravity in a flat spacetime, focusing on the relation between the Einstein Hilbert action and the covariant volume form. We find that all methods are equivalent to multiplying the Einstein-Hilbert action by a constant. Our analysis also identifies two distinct ways of relativistic generalization for particles and strings.

This study presents advancements in three-dimensional image retrieval by utilizing symmetric multi-resolution geometric analysis, which efficiently deals with complex, highly distorted 3D image data. Our research includes the development of a robust, symmetric image matching technique using SP-Sym models, which effectively resistant to distortions. This method's performance is evaluated using the Colmap software's reconstructed models. Our results demonstrate outstanding resistance to partial occlusions, geometric distortions, and limited viewpoints, outperforming existing techniques such as 3D-SIFT by approximately 100%. Additionally, we introduce a novel approach for 3D image abstractions, which enables accurate automatic registration of unlabelled images. Our technique relies on sparse local features derived from image volumes rather than surface approximations. This method's novel application in image processing allows automatic grouping of image volumes based on their semantic content.

We have obtained UV and optical light curve data from various space missions including Kepler, TESS, and POETS, which enabled us to investigate the behavior of the central white dwarf in the double-degenerate system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19. The system has a 40.5 minutes period and exhibits pronounced superposed pulsations in all observed bands. Utilizing various models and assuming an white dwarf mass of 0.85 M$_{\odot}$, we were able to determine individual pulse amplitudes and phases for each band. According to our analysis, the overall pulse amplitude in the UV and optical regions are found to be 0.032 and 0.013 magnitudes respectively. The 160-day long oscillations in the optical and UV brightness are consistent with a single variable component, which varies by about 0.10 and 0.14 magnitudes in the U and B bands respectively. We found that this variable component is likely caused by atmospheric convective eddies induced by the 16.6 day oscillation in ring variable accretion rate.

This study reevaluates global aggregation methods by applying optimal transport theory, resulting in a new class of node-weighted aggregation operators beyond traditional mean-based aggregators. It specifically identifies linear combinations of weighted means to be the unique solutions to the averaged cost function, and demonstrates that these operators fulfill significant mathematical properties. Furthermore, this work also establishes relationships between these new aggregators and existing ones, and explores their connections with the mean-based aggregators under specific weight constraints.

The growing sample of Type I and II Active Galactic Nuclei allows for a detailed analysis of host galaxy characteristics, including morphological features and optical magnitudes, through the application of the GALEX View-FRT pipeline. By utilizing View-FRT's data, the following study differentiates between AGN populations based on host galaxy properties and telescope orientation. Notably, the study reveals that LINERs tend to have more prominent spiral structures and brighter optical emissions compared to other AGN types, while they also exhibit a broader range of star-forming features. Additionally, the analysis shows that the distribution of galaxy types and host galaxy properties do not correlate in a meaningful way. Furthermore, the study finds that AGN populations show varying tendencies based on telescope orientation: Type I Infrared Galaxies and LINERs appear more common when viewed edge-on, whereas Type II AGN are more frequently observed when viewed side-on. By contrast, the study finds that the orientation of AGN does not significantly affect the distribution of Type I AGN or Seyferts.

This research achieves a novel goal by accurately differentiating between hypersurfaces, specifically rotational planes in four-dimensional Euclidean space, using a unique geometric approach based on a customized Gaussian function that adapts to the geometry of these surfaces. Our methodology employs several key steps: First, we define a customized Gaussian function that is tailored to the unique characteristics of rotational planes in four-dimensional Euclidean space. Next, we establish an optimal distortion parameter, also known as a weight function, that is sensitive to the geometry of these surfaces. Our findings also reveal that a specific distortion parameter, which we have developed, is capable of accurately differentiating between rotational planes in four-dimensional Euclidean space. Additionally, we have demonstrated that our customized Gaussian function is sufficient to determine (or recover) the orientation of these surfaces.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires significant effort and can be a major obstacle in the development of new segmentation models. Pre-training on large publicly available datasets such as OpenStreetMap is a common technique used to enhance neural network performance. In this study, we examine whether depth estimation or image classification pre-training is more beneficial for semantic segmentation. Notably, we find that depth estimation outperforms image classification despite the limited scope of our dataset. Additionally, we observe improvements in low-disparity areas and attribute the enhanced performance to the disparity map's effectiveness in guiding the segmentation process.

Transformers have revolutionized the field of natural language processing, outperforming other architectures in various tasks such as machine translation, summarization, and text classification. However, their application to time-series data, particularly in the field of multimedia, has been limited. To bridge this gap, we present TCube, a novel multimedia storytelling system that leverages domain-agnostic Transformers to generate engaging, coherent, and detailed stories based on time-stamped data. Unlike existing approaches, TCube can adapt to various domains without requiring modifications to the model architecture itself. Instead, it incorporates multiple innovative techniques, including multi-modal multi-task training, to produce high-quality stories in real-time. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of TCube, demonstrating superior performance on multiple storytelling datasets.

The ATLAS experiment examines the CP behaviour of beauty mesons to understand violations of CP symmetry. Analyses were conducted to assess violations of CP symmetry in the decay of $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ mesons into intermediate states not influenced by strong interactions, as well as in rare uncoupled decays of $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ mesons. Findings from these analyses are in line with predictions from the Standard Model, though not sufficiently precise to detect potential anomalies. Crucially, the data discussed here were all obtained utilizing integrated luminosity of 16.4 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ provided by the LHC at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Future research will focus on enhancing precision by increasing luminosity, as well as by collecting data at various centre-of-mass energies to explore violations of CP symmetry in $B^0_s$ mesons decoupling into different intermediate states.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel mildly periodic measures that are distinct from the traditional Gibbs measures. We achieve this by introducing a novel symmetry group with specific properties, thereby expanding the existing classification of periodic measures in this model.

This research addresses the issue of well-posedness for a broad class of first-order hyperbolic partial differential equations with variable coefficients, given the constraint of initial data being relatively small in certain higher-order derivatives. Although the coefficients have strong tendencies of growth in space, they have a significant improvement in decay rate when considering time, which is verified to be sufficient for achieving global in-time stability of the solution. This finding significantly expands upon existing outcomes in the field.

This research presents a novel Japanese Word Division (JWD) model that surpasses current standards. Unlike typical word division systems, our model is designed to handle uncommon or unseen word divisions during training. Building upon the success of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) in language models, we developed an Extended Short-Term Memory (ExSTM) network for JWD. ExSTM's additional gate mechanisms enable it to effectively capture long-term, cross-word dependencies in JWD. Furthermore, we introduce a new training method that adjusts non-existent time steps, allowing our model to be entirely trainable end-to-end. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our ExSTM-based model achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and generalizability.

So-called "knowledge sharing" is the act of dividing information. On the other hand, "information exchange" refers to the act of acquiring knowledge. A platform's effectiveness in fostering knowledge sharing and information exchange is closely tied to its external links. These links serve as a bridge between the platform and the wider world, supplying users with novel information. This study seeks to understand the role of these external links by analyzing popular knowledge-sharing and information-exchange destinations on Stack Overflow. Our analysis reveals that external links are predominantly utilized by high-reputation users and that these shared resources are mainly technical in nature. Furthermore, we find that external links are often associated with informative responses and that their implementation could involve automatic content copying or manual content pasting. Our results suggest that such implementation could also be gauged by the level of involvement from the original source authors.

The galaxy diversity issue remains a major obstacle in the development of artificial intelligence (AI) systems capable of informed decision-making, as inputs from diverse sources can cause outputs to be unstable and unpredictable. Current solutions propose altering either the system outputs or the environment in which the outputs are given, but a critical examination of these approaches reveals that they address different forms of output variability separately. Neither class directly addresses the root cause of instability, which is the inconsistent interpretation of inputs. A new method is presented that focuses on processing inputs in a unified manner to produce consistent outputs. This approach is then evaluated against the existing solutions by determining which one reduces output variability when applied to actual decision-making datasets.

Although climate change communication is a pressing issue, public engagement remains a challenge. Research has shown that limited knowledge of climate facts leads to lethargic public response. Our research aims to revitalize climate conversation through a comprehensive climate information repository that bridges the gap between basic climate knowledge and in-depth scientific research. This climate data repository is designed as an interactive tool, providing various visualization options and gamified elements to enhance effective climate engagement and promote climate awareness.

Medical research significantly benefits from extracting symptom and treatment information from unstructured medical records, and various deep learning-based approaches have been developed to achieve this. However, the performance of these models is typically confined to a single hospital or a limited set of institutions due to their vulnerability to source bias. This research addresses the challenge of domain generalization for extracting symptoms and treatment information from various clinical settings. A proposed multi-task framework enables the simultaneous extraction of symptoms, treatments, and medical specialties from unstructured notes, and we integrate it with a source domain adaptation module to overcome source bias. The proposed method demonstrates exceptional performance across diverse hospitals and outperforms comparative methods in extracting symptoms and treatments.

Deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising technique for training self-driving cars. A successful implementation involves using scenes observed from the vehicle and mapping capabilities to extract features, which are then fed into a reinforcement learning agent. This agent leverages historical data to learn a strategy for navigating through various situations. By iterating between the training process and system testing on a simulator or real-world platform, the self-driving system can refine its in-field behavior.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in various tasks. However, these models have several significant drawbacks, including (1) the vast computational resources required for their development and operation, (2) the enormous energy consumption caused by the frequent switching of electrical currents, and (3) the challenge of explaining their decisions due to the lack of transparency. To address these issues, we examine the potential of bio-inspired spiking neural networks as an alternative to traditional AI networks. Our research reveals that these networks, despite having fewer neurons compared to their competitors, can accurately classify complex patterns and simultaneously minimize computational load and energy expenditure by selectively firing neurons. Moreover, our results show that these networks consistently provide consistent results with minimal deviation, explaining their decisions clearly through the analysis of neuron firing sequences.

This study examines the characteristics of strange quark stars under the influence of a spin aligned magnetic field at an elevated temperature. The quark star's equation of state is based on the Gogopinath and Chakrabarti model, and we utilize the Mean Field Theory to analyze the thermodynamic properties of the quark star in terms of specific free energy, charge density, spin aligned pressure, and energy density in relation to central density and temperature. Additionally, we investigate the mass-radius relationship of the quark star in response to a spin aligned magnetic field and temperature variations.

A surge in artificial intelligence (AI) utilization across computing devices has sparked a pressing need to leverage underutilized resources like smartphones and tablets to accelerate AI model training. To bridge this gap, we've developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing network that enables contributions from individual users via a web interface. By allowing computations to be segmented into bite-sized chunks, Pando facilitates seamless and frictionless contributions from any device with a modern browser. Our core architecture comprises a cloud-based gateway, a lightweight mobile application, and a adaptable computing process, all of which work in harmony to maximize productivity. Pando's individual-focused, browser-agnostic approach sets it apart from existing volunteer computing networks like BOINC, enabling us to gather valuable insights into user behavior and computational capabilities. Furthermore, Pando's modular design fosters a highly customizable and scalable environment for running a wide range of use cases, including but not limited to, training deep learning models and data encryption. With Pando's volunteer computing network, we've demonstrated substantial computational gains, with a notable 10% enhancement in training time for a specified deep learning model across participating users' devices.

This research presents an innovative non-parametric approach to estimating non-linear eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a complex phenomenon modelled by a non-linear equation based on noisy data. The method utilizes an interpolation technique to approximate the eigenfunctions of the operator, with the challenge of non-uniqueness resolved by incorporating initial conditions. The estimation procedure is split into two components: determining the eigenfunctions and eigenvectors. The first component employs an optimization process to estimate the eigenfunctions, with convergence rates analyzed and confidence intervals established. The second component, involving the estimation of eigenvectors, is tackled by minimizing a discrepancy measure between observed data and predicted outcomes, with a convergence rate analysis and confidence intervals also derived for this case. The study conducts extensive numerical experiments to assess the performance of the proposed methods under various noise levels and sampling strategies.

We establish a connection between intermediate $\beta$-shifts and avaricious $\beta$-shifts with a gap. This relationship enables us to derive the entropy of intermediate $\beta$-shifts as a solution to a certain equation involving the derivative of a x-ray transform.

We investigate the dynamics of a vector flavor $SO(N_f = 2)$ gauge theory, $ SO(N_c) \with N_f = 2$, in the regime where a large IR cutoff is imposed. The theory features an inherent global $SO(2N_f)$ symmetry and an exceptional $SU(2)_R$ symmetry unique to $SO(N_f)$ flavors, leading to an intricate interplay between these symmetries and the $SO(N_f)$ global symmetry, causing difficulties in analysis. To circumvent this issue, we introduce a flavor symmetry twist, $SO(N_f) \to U(2) \times U(2)$. Under this modification, we demonstrate the existence of two distinct phases: (I) a confined phase, characterized by a broken $SU(2)_R$ symmetry and an intact $SO(2N_f)$ global symmetry; (II) a deconfined phase, marked by $\pi_2 - \mathcal{E} \ne 0$, $\pi_1 - \mathcal{E} = 0$, and restoration of $SU(2)_R$ symmetry. Furthermore, we derive and analyze an effective, two-form Abelian gauge theory in the twisted theory, and discuss the novel phenomenon of 't Hooft anomaly inflation. Additionally, we discuss possible generalizations to more intricate flavor groups, such as $SO(N_f = 3)$.

Machine learning models like random forests and boosted trees achieve high accuracy but are difficult to understand due to their complex nature. We develop a new visualization method, attribution graphs, to help interpret these models by highlighting key feature interactions. In addition to revealing important individual features, our method identifies feature subsets and patterns, such as correlations and nonlinear relationships, contributing to model decisions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through examples and examine its reliability, also highlighting how attribution graphs can be used for feature engineering and improving model performance.

Securely processing data, especially sensitive information, is crucial for various applications. conventional approaches rely heavily on general-purpose CPUs, which expose memory contents and compromise security, but using specialized TEEs like SGX for training brings its own set of limitations and complexities. This research introduces Flatee, an innovative federated learning framework that allows cross-domain training across TEEs without restricting models to specific languages or platforms. It presents an extensible architecture, a formalized training protocol, and comprehensive evaluations, showcasing Flatee's efficiency and scalability in several real-world scenarios.

A scalable solution is proposed for evaluating robotic operators across various configurations, starting with a basic embedded system suitable for widespread adoption.
A novel approach utilizes a low-cost Raspberry Pi 4 for operational purposes, allowing for the exploration of automated evaluation methods without compromising performance.
By automating the process, the automated evaluator can assess performance more efficiently than human operators, providing more accurate and reliable results with minimal distortion.
Moreover, the automated evaluator's openness facilitates the development of adaptable code, enabling easy modifications to optimize its performance in accordance with specific application requirements.

This research introduces Timeloops, an automated framework for adapting system call policies in containerized microservices at runtime. The objective is to enhance security by limiting privileged access to specific system resources. However, manually creating system call policies is a complex, error-prone task that may result in over-restrictive policies hindering performance or over-permissive policies exposing the application to security risks. To address these challenges, Timeloops leverages machine learning and runtime data collection to dynamically shape system call policies without requiring advance system configuration. By balancing performance and security, Timeloops seeks to provide efficient and effective microservice adaptation.

In geometry of commerce, we examine linear classification in spaces of commodity, such as the Bertini variety, product of projective lines, and Fano varieties. Our study focuses on the linear classifier's kernel, which is a section of a specific line bundle. We establish that linear classifiers on these spaces are uniquely defined up to a multiplicity factor and investigate how this uniqueness changes with varying combinatorial parameters. Additionally, we explore the connections between linear classification in commodity space and linear classification in other contexts, such as linear programming, real space with constrained coordinates, and the Grassmannian.

Past research has found that the regular patterns of stars orbiting around a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy like the bulge of the Milky Way can be complex and not easily explained. Building on previous studies, we have developed a new approach to understanding these patterns by dividing the orbits of stars into different groups based on their eccentricity and studying their distributions individually. Our findings reveal significant variations in the arrangements of stars depending on their eccentricities, with certain orbital patterns showing clumps and others being evenly spaced. These results disagree with previous models that predicted uniform distributions of stars regardless of their orbits, but align with the findings of an earlier study that initially observed these patterns, even though they were initially dismissed as an outlier.

This work presents a method called Random Model Predictive Control to efficiently operate large-scale battery energy storage systems. A specific approach is demonstrated using a detailed residential building simulation, which incorporates a power flow routine and optimization problem that minimizes operating costs. Our proposed algorithm limits the number of possible operating points for the battery and only recovers from exceptions, thereby reducing computational demands. A comparative study examines the performance of RMPC in conjunction with power flow-based models, and considers the impact of varying exception handling strategies and model inaccuracies.

Independent component analysis offers a powerful framework for tackling high-dimensional data sets despite the intricacies posed by noise and its unknown statistical characteristics. Our focus lies on noise that follows a Gaussian distribution, and we provide a non-parametric approach for determining the transformation matrix, which in turn facilitates the recovery of the underlying independent components. To achieve this, we formulate the problem as an optimization problem, and through analysis, demonstrate the existence of the optimal solution and its unique characteristics. Building on these findings, we then explore various optimization techniques, and conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the performance of different algorithms. Interestingly, our results show that utilizing sparse regularization can lead to accurate results even in the presence of limited data, and thus provide a reliable method for high-dimensional data analysis.

A novel variant of the voter model is introduced, which incorporates a competition-colonization tradeoff into the dynamics of a multi-species system. This model is studied using both deterministic and stochastic dynamics. In the deterministic setting, an extensive study of species interactions is conducted via extensive numerical analysis. In the stochastic setting, an in-depth examination of the model's behavior is performed via Monte Carlo simulations, resulting in a comprehensive phase diagram that outlines possible outcomes such as species annihilation, diverse ecological coexistence, and chaotic population dynamics including interdependent and independent population fluctuations. Furthermore, the obtained phase diagram is compared with existing results from the literature on similar ecological models.

In the context of an abelian quantum double model, regional von Neumann algebras play a crucial role in establishing relationships between local subsets of the state space $D$. The quantum double $D^{\circ}$ serves as the category consisting of regions $I$ and intertwiners between representations, acting as morphisms. The functorial properties of the state-to-field correspondence, $\Phi: D \to D^{\circ}$, are then examined to see how it preserves the structure of local algebras and intertwiners across boundaries. Specifically, it can be seen that $\Phi$ takes marginal restrictions of subregions $I \subset I_1 \cup I_2$ and intertwiners connecting them to morphisms in $D^{\circ}$, that are associated with the composite region $I \cdot I_2$. The proof of this involves showing that the images of local algebras and intertwiners on $D$ are subcategories of $D^{\circ}$. The state-to-field correspondence $\Phi$ is seen as a functor that maps the category of local algebras and intertwiners on $D$ to a subcategory consisting of special morphisms in $D^{\circ}$. The conformal quantum field theory based on this model is then seen to be equivalent to the category algebra $D^{\circ}_{I}$.

To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we propose a coherent feedback circuit system. The entanglement between the system's components can be quantified using logarithmic negativity. Our findings indicate that the proposed setup achieves greater entanglement than traditional cavity magnomechanics, achieving a strong entanglement regime with less thermal photons. Furthermore, we observe that the entanglement's stability and overall quantity can be controlled through the cavity's transmittance and reflectance.

This work compiles previous research on one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators, providing full expressions in dimensional regularization for both space- and penultimate-configurations. The findings are further enhanced by deriving corresponding expressions for the most relevant components of the splitting operators, bringing anti-Feinberg ordering to both the α-zeta and α-phi forms. In addition, an innovative set of rules is proposed to facilitate the conversion between these different representations, streamlining the process.

The Neron Desingularization (Neron 1953) is a significant algebraic tool utilized for eliminating inconsistencies in one dimensional local rings with imperfect residue fields. Over the course of the past 60 years, the Neron Desingularization has undergone significant enhancements in its application and computational methods. A more recent and advanced adaptation of the Neron Desingularization is known as Positive General Neron Desingularization (P.G.N.D.), which was first introduced and explained in detail by Schrader and Vishne (2011). The primary focus of this paper is to provide a comprehensive proof and detailed explanation of the P.G.N.D algorithm, specifically for use in one dimensional local rings.

Ancient people utilized sundials to tell time before the widespread use of clocks, and these devices remain an important cultural heritage today, albeit largely overlooked in modern society. In an effort to document and promote sundials as a significant cultural asset, a photo contest and database were launched in 2019 under the name Suryakala-Nusantara, aiming to capture sundials across Indonesia's vast archipelago, an estimated 1,743 islands. The project not only showcases the beauty of sundials but also highlights the country's rich history and cultural diversity, utilizing Google Maps and MyMap educational tools for interactive mapping and storytelling. The ultimate goal is to create a comprehensive map of sundials by 2025, marking Indonesia's 75th independence anniversary, and serve as a valuable educational platform for youngsters to develop digital mapping and storytelling skills.

This research proposes a new method for increased intelligence in IoT networks by leveraging a reflective surface and an integrated information network. A novel non-reflective area of the surface is determined using a smart optimization technique, enabling more efficient channel utilization and increased connectivity in the network. The proposed fully-digital approach eliminates computational complexity and provides accurate probability distribution. The results demonstrate that this method achieves optimal outage probability performance with reduced complexity.

The pandemic-driven shortage of LDV instruments has highlighted the limitations of current research using a single LDV system to acquire two-dimensional data, especially in studies of turbulent flows in non-fixed coordinates. This paper addresses this issue by demonstrating the feasibility of obtaining full two-dimensional velocity data in free space using a single LDV system, without the need for additional equipment. By employing a complex mathematical approach and a sophisticated laser-based technique, we successfully developed an innovative method that can accurately track particles in three-dimensional flow conditions. This innovative method was then applied to the study of turbulent flows in two-dimensional conditions, and the resulting data were compared to established research in the field, including both numerical models and experimental data obtained using different techniques. The application of this innovative method to the study of turbulent flows in non-fixed coordinates has opened up new avenues for researchers to utilize existing data to gain a deeper understanding of these complex flows.

The paper explores the concept of spectra based on relations rather than maps, specifically focusing on first-order theories. It demonstrates that any first-order theory can be associated with an equivalence relation that captures its key model-theoretic properties. This relationship enables a semigroup of classes represented by matrices, which have entries defined by formulas. Furthermore, it is established that classes of models, defined by arbitrary first-order sentences, correspond to ideals within this semigroup, thereby reinterpreting fundamental ideas in model theory through a novel algebraic lens.

The effectiveness of an electrostatic phase disc in mitigating aberrations in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs) was evaluated. By simulating the phase disc using different voltage profiles and observing the outcomes for various underfocused and overfocused conditions, our research revealed that such a disc can be utilized as an aberration corrector. Our findings also suggest that manufacturing techniques precision to the order of a tenth of an angstrom would be required to achieve noticeable improvement.

In 1765, Euler sent a letter to Diderot, addressing concerns raised by the French mathematician and philosopher Lazare Carnot about the lack of rigorous foundation in calculus. Carnot's criticisms were based on the criticism of calculus made by the influential Enlightenment thinker and critic of metaphysics, Immanuel Kant. Kant's criticisms were detailed in his 1768 book "On the Radical Evil in Human Nature," where he argued that calculus relied heavily on vague concepts, making it incompatible with a logical, precise mathematical system. Euler, however, successfully refuted Kant's claims in the 1770 letter. Euler's point being that assessment or calculation methods do not necessarily affect the truth or falsehood of a concept. This letter was later included in Euler's works published from 1769 to 1772.

We provide a direct proof of a combinatorial formula enumerating points in a $d$-dimensional unit sphere centered at the origin in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, using the $L_1$-norm. The formula is given by $\sum_{k=0}^{\left\lfloor \frac{d}{2}\right\rfloor} \binom{d}{2k} k! (\binom{2k+q-1}{k})^2$, where $q$ represents the dimension's parity, which has been previously validated via stochastic walks.

Our investigation into spherically symmetric black holes begins with a review of the impact of holonomy constraints on the expanded geometry of black holes. We then focus on the Gambo-Olmedo-Pullin black hole as a particularly interesting case, due to its spatially non-compact polymer nature. For GO-P black holes with zero or infinite bulk bond dimensions, our analysis reduces to the more familiar models of Schwarzschild and polymer black holes, respectively. Conversely, the quasinormal spectrum of the GO-P black hole lies within the intermediate range. With the exception of the $l=0,1$ modes, the quasinormal frequencies of the GO-P black hole can be approximated by interpolating between the corresponding frequencies of the Schwarzschild and polymer black holes. The outcome of our investigation implies that the effect of the quantum phase shift on the black hole's near-horizon structure is moderate.

In graphene panels with edge doping, the presence of phonon-mediated long-range interactions between electrons beyond the standard Coulomb force is a key phenomenon. When the temperature or electron density exceeds the characteristic energy scale of the panels, defined as $\gamma=\gamma_0(n_0)e^{-\lambda_0/(k_B T)}$, where $n_0$ is the undoped density and $\lambda_0$ is the Luke-Nielson constant, this new force starts to resemble the standard Coulomb interaction. However, at lower temperatures, the unique shielded interaction results in significant deviations from the standard mean-field description of doped graphene, including the disappearance of the celebrated "bee-hive" structure in the density of states and the emergence of four-fold symmetry in the density of states at the magic angle. Moreover, the unique interaction effects can potentially be experimentally verified through measurements of thermal conductivity or specific heat. Specifically, we predict that the specific heat will be reduced by a factor of $1-\frac{\gamma_0}{\gamma_1}(\frac{k_B T}{\mu})^2$, where $\mu$ is the chemical potential and $\mu\approx\sqrt{\gamma_1 k_B T}$, where $\gamma_1$ is the Evers-Dossmann-Probst-Maschke constant, indicating that the specific heat is reduced compared to the standard mean-field description.

The quality of generated speech from text-to-speech models heavily depends on the accuracy of word-level alignments, which can be compromised in noisy environments. The Masked Dialogue model addresses this limitation by employing a masking technique that samples frames from the target speech feature sequence and trains a autoencoder to generate replacement frames from the masked frames in the adjacent context. The proposed approach is evaluated on speech synthesis tasks and demonstrates the ability to mitigate errors caused by speech corruption or ill-formulated text. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the Masked Dialogue model is effective in learning robust word-level frames even from short sentences synthesis.

We develop an innovative approach to reasoning in high-dimensional spaces by utilizing hidden variable projection predictive variables. This method employs Gaussian process regression on latent variables, enabling efficient use of limited functional data. We derive predictive distributions for observed variables and hidden variables, then propose a range of predictors and regressors based on optimality criteria. We investigate the asymptotic properties of these estimators and predictors through theoretical analysis. To facilitate practical application, we develop algorithms for maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian sampling of model parameters. The method's performance is demonstrated through simulation studies. Furthermore, we provide examples of using this approach to analyze real-world datasets, highlighting its utility.

In recent years, deep learning technologies have achieved significant advancements across various computational domains; however, they remain vulnerable to data poisoning attacks which can lead to severe security breaches during training processes. While research has primarily focused on coordinate-based poisoning attacks against machine learning models, a new study investigates the feasibility of launching active attacks through a third-party adversarial entity intercepting communication channels between clients and servers. Specifically, this entity can carry out additive and substitution data poisoning attacks via a malicious generative framework, and it is demonstrated that these attacks can successfully compromise the robustness of machine learning models in remote access and software-based protection scenarios.

Climate change denial has become a widespread issue, thriving in online environments where conspiracy theories can spread easily. This study examines the most common conspiracy theories circulating on social media by analyzing large datasets from Twitter and Reddit. It investigates the core themes of these conspiracy theories and explores the tactics used to promote them online. Furthermore, we assess the impact of these conspiracy theories on climate change discourse and consider the challenges of addressing them.

Proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV were monitored to investigate the appearance of shadow matter, a hypothesized type of matter, by looking at its decay into one or two muons and dijet or Z boson-jet combinations.  The search utilized data recorded by the CMS experiment in 2016, totaling 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of accumulated luminosity.  The study set a range of new restrictions on the cross-section of shadow matter production, and it placed the first limit on the cross-section of single-production, ranging from 0.15 pb to 0.65 pb based on a specific mass range and interaction strength.  The study also placed the first two-particle-production constraints, with a minimum limit on the cross-section ranging from 0.25 pb to 0.75 pb based on a specific mass range and interaction strength.

Given a finitely generated algebra, we establish that the category of its finitely generated right $R$-modules exhibits Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if the category of finitely generated left $R$-modules does. Furthermore, we extend Serre duality to categories with finite injective dimension, which enables us to derive a consequence involving the dimension of the injective dimension for modules in such categories.

Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work that expanded the use of LATE in fields of study to account for uncertainty in treatment likelihood, we apply this concept to the IV identification framework as a whole. This involves demonstrating that for any given (potentially complex) treatment rule and noisy treatment data, there exists a corresponding LATE that can be reliably estimated through data analysis. To illustrate this idea, we use a data set from Norway to investigate how the military's conscript program affects the income of university graduates, taking into account the likely diverse impacts of serving in different fields.

A cutting-edge research proposal utilizing the EIC, collider, and neutrino facilities is presented, focusing on delivering the world's most precise measurements of low-energy antineutron-proton, kaon-nucleon, and other important interactions. A novel beamline is described that uses J/psi ions produced by a Lambertson magnetic lens to generate a high-precision antiparticle beam. The feasibility of producing a high-intensity antineutron beam is also explored. The experiments envisioned will not only provide highly accurate data on antiparticle-nucleon interactions but also open doors to innovative research in antimatter physics, including the creation of ultracold antineutron optics and a next-generation antineutron beamline.

Most formed stars reside in stellar triple system configurations, especially those with a disk. Our research centers around the accretion rates in such systems, backed by simulations, to understand how they are influenced by the masses of the secondary and tertiary components. Initial findings indicate that secondary stars with masses between approximately 0.2 to 10 times the mass of the Sun tend to slow down the primary's accretion rate in protoplanetary disks, compared to isolated star systems. This reduction is more pronounced for lower-mass secondary stars. Our models also suggest that disk disruption tends to decrease the primary's accretion rate more significantly when the mass ratio of the secondary and tertiary components is higher. Ultimately, these systems may experience extended star formation periods due to lowered accretion rates.

The concept of inherent flatness is examined in lattice cosmology, focusing on its mathematical implications. Two types of inherent flatness are identified: (i) the standard type, which occurs when the lattice's Hamiltonian is path-integral divergent; (ii) a new type, which arises when the Hamiltonian's quantum fluctuations cause its cosmological scale to diverge. Both of these cases lead to the simplification that the Hamiltonian's classical potential is constant. Furthermore, it is found that the first case can be transformed into the second by selecting an appropriate UV cutoff. It is also observed that inherent flatness is preserved when the lattice cosmical scale is used as the expansion parameter in a renormalization group analysis. Finally, it is noted that the first case can be associated with the presence of dark matter, which is responsible for the scale's divergence.

This study presents an innovative image modeling technique that integrates multiple images into a single representation. The images within the representation are segmented and linked by geometrically compatible partitioning. The method's objective function quantifies image similarity and relevance through regional segmentation and representation matching, while also accounting for the availability and quality of data. By utilizing a non-parametric approach, the technique can analyze various types of image data without presupposing their structure. The approach can successfully divide images into compatible components, even in the presence of missing information, and has applications in fields such as computer vision and geology where image partitioning can reveal valuable insights.

The phenomenon of superradiance is predicted to occur in rotating black holes and white dwarfs. Recent observations of massive quasars, which involve the measurement of spin alignment, offer a potential means to detect the ultralight bosons driving this process.
